text.text: A ten-minute tour of the festival in this workspace. Share it with programmers, pre-screeners, guest services and venue managers.

Month before: every copy tested, every guest booked
Festival week: 9 am stand-up with venues, guests and box office

Programmers own selection and the programme. Pre-screeners own their scores. Guest services owns invitations, travel and hotels. Venue managers own tech checks and screening day. The festival director reads the whole picture and decides on awards logistics.
Screener links are for review only and never shared. Nobody scores a film by someone they know. Every filmmaker hears our decision from us, by email, before the line-up is public.

text.text: A festival year runs on fixed dates. Filmmakers plan around your deadlines, and everything after the call for entries works backwards from opening night.
Nine to six months out: call for entries
Open submissions with three deadlines: early, regular and late, each with its own
. Offer fee waivers for local and student filmmakers.
Set the categories and the premiere rules. Many festivals give priority to world and North American premieres in competition.
Recruit pre-screeners and give them the scoring guide.
Six to three months out: screening the entries
Every submission gets at least two
scores before the late deadline closes.
Programmers watch everything scoring 7 or above, plus anything with a split verdict.

Daily stand-up at 9 am with venue managers, guest services and the box office. Award winners are decided by the jury before closing night.
Pay filmmakers' screening fees, return copies, send thank-you notes and a survey to audiences and guests. Write down what to change while it is fresh.

A world-premiere feature was withdrawn six weeks out when it sold to a streamer. The waitlisted Cornfield Opera's director had already declined, so programmers moved the strongest short documentary into the slot and told ticket holders the same day.
Hundreds of filmmakers trust you with their work. Pre-screening is how every one of them gets a fair, attentive viewing, even when there are a thousand entries.
Each film gets at least two pre-screeners, one of whom knows the category well.

show on each film. Programmers watch every film averaging 7 or more and every film where two scorers disagree by three points or more. Scores guide; programmers decide.
Juries score only films in competition, after the festival screening, against the award criteria. Jury scores and notes stay confidential until the awards are announced.
Some festivals offer short notes to declined filmmakers. Write every note as if the filmmaker will read it, because they may.

A Quiet Harvest scored 8 from one pre-screener while the second score is overdue. The programmer reassigned it to a third reader to keep the decide-by date, and both scores arrived in time for Thursday's programming meeting.
Every screening during festival week follows the same routine. Audiences remember a late start or a missing subtitle far longer than the film.

If anything goes wrong with picture or sound, the projectionist stops, the host apologizes, and the film restarts from a scene change.
